security_spec.violation_condition: In the FreeBSD kernel, when a code-patching or module-loading sequence performs multiple stores to modify instruction memory and the Ziccid 'eventual visibility' property causes an instruction fetch to observe a partially-complete store chain before the final FENCE.I barrier executes — particularly on cacheable, coherent memory regions where Ziccid applies — the hart may execute half-patched instructions (e.g., a partially-written branch target, an uninitialized immediate field, or an in-progress nop-sled). FreeBSD's pmap_kenter or vtophys-based code update paths that assume FENCE.I is the sole mechanism for I-fetch visibility are unsynchronized against this eventuality.
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: Multiple sequential store instructions (sb/sh/sw/sd) to a writable+executable kernel page, followed by a non-atomic FENCE.I or delayed FENCE.I, where the cumulative write crosses instruction boundaries — grep for consecutive stores to pages mapped VM_PROT_EXECUTE or consecutive stores preceding fence_i calls in machine-dependent code.
security_spec.summary: Ziccid removes the hard FENCE.I gating invariant: stores to I-stream memory become progressively visible to the local hart's fetch stage in program order, so multi-store kernel code patches are exposed to a TOCTOU race between partial-store visibility and the final FENCE.I flush — FreeBSD's module loader and live-patching paths must ensure all stores precede a single FENCE.I without intermediary instruction fetches landing in the patched region

findings.finding: R_RISCV_JAL relocation performs 4 sequential stores (*insn32p = insert_imm(...)) to the same instruction word on a writable+executable kernel module page, with no fence_i() before or after. Under Ziccid 'eventual visibility', an instruction fetch on any hart can observe partially-modified intermediate states (e.g., only bits [20:31] patched but bits [1:10] still stale). elf_cpu_load_file() (line 536) is an empty stub. Combined with link_elf.c:preload_protect1() excluding RISC-V (line 807 guard), module text pages remain RWX throughout relocation, creating a privilege_escape window where half-patched instructions (corrupt JAL immediates) are executable.

R_RISCV_CALL relocation performs 2 sequential stores to a 2-instruction AUIPC+JALR pair (insn32p[0] and insn32p[1]) on writable+executable module text, with no fence_i() barrier. A hart fetching this sequence during the window between the AUIPC store (line 400) and JALR store (line 404) will execute a new-AUIPC + old-JALR hybrid, computing a corrupt target address. This is a privilege_escape vector — the corrupted PC-relative computation can branch to attacker-controlled kernel addresses.

R_RISCV_PCREL_LO12_S relocation performs 2 sequential stores to the same 32-bit instruction word (insert_imm splitting the immediate across bits [5:25] and [0:7]), with no fence_i(). Intermediate store state exposes a partially-constructed S-type immediate, producing a corrupt store instruction (wrong offset) or a different opcode entirely if bit 5 is in flux.

R_RISCV_LO12_S relocation: same multi-store pattern as PCREL_LO12_S — two sequential stores to the same instruction word on executable module text with no fence_i(). Same privilege_escape consequence.

elf_cpu_load_file() is a no-op stub (returns 0). This is the arch-specific hook where a post-relocation icache sync should be performed. After elf_reloc_internal() completes all instruction-modifying stores, no fence_i() or pmap_sync_icache() is ever called in the module load path. Compare with arm64/amd64 which handle protection changes via preload_protect1() in link_elf.c. The RISC-V kernel module loader is missing the architecturally-required FENCE.I barrier before executing relocated code.

preload_protect1() applies pmap protection changes after module load on __aarch64__ and __amd64__, but RISC-V is explicitly excluded (hits the no-op #else at line 835). This means kernel module text pages remain VM_PROT_WRITE|VM_PROT_EXECUTE (RWX) during and after relocation. While this function is about protection rather than icache sync, the RWX mapping is what enables the elf_reloc_internal multi-store writes to be visible to instruction fetch in the first place. Enabling this for RISC-V would reduce the attack surface, though it doesn't fix the missing fence_i.

db_write_bytes() writes breakpoint bytes one-at-a-time via a byte-store loop (line 151-152) to executable kernel pages, then calls fence_i() at line 155. The byte-by-byte store pattern means a partial breakpoint instruction (1-3 bytes written) could be speculatively fetched by the local hart before the fence_i barrier completes. Other harts are stopped via IPI_STOP at DDB entry. Risk is low since the hart is in the debugger context (not executing the patched region), but a speculative icache fill of a partially-written EBREAK encoding could produce an unexpected trap on DDB resume.

Single memcpy() of a complete 4-byte JAL instruction into the tracepoint, immediately followed by fence_i(). The single aligned 4-byte store is architecturally atomic on RV64, so no partial-instruction window exists. Compliant with the RISC-V FENCE.I requirements.
Single memcpy() of a complete 4-byte NOP, immediately followed by fence_i(). Same atomic-store argument as sdt_tracepoint_patch. Compliant.

Single direct store (2-byte uint16_t for C.EBREAK or 4-byte uint32_t for EBREAK) into the patchpoint, with fence_i() immediately following on the adjacent line. The code takes one of two exclusive paths (FBT_C_PATCHVAL or FBT_PATCHVAL), each performing exactly one store before fence_i(). Compliant.
Same pattern as FBT: single direct store (2 or 4 bytes) into patchpoint, fence_i() immediately after. One store per execution path. Compliant.

Three kinst_memcpy() calls to a freshly-allocated trampoline page (kp_tramp), with a single fence_i() at the end. The trampoline page has never been executed, so no stale icache entries exist. The final fence_i() ensures all stores are visible before the trampoline is first executed. Compliant.

Issues fence_i() on the local hart after the GDB stub writes breakpoint bytes to kernel memory. The comment correctly notes remote harts sync their icache when resuming from IPI_STOP. The local fence_i() is architecturally sufficient for the writing hart. Compliant in isolation, though it depends on the GDB byte-write path (gdb_packet.c) to have completed all stores before calling this.

Simple fence_i() wrapper used by membarrier for userland JIT icache sync requests (MEMBARRIER_CMD_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED_SYNC_CORE). Correctly issues FENCE.I on the calling hart. No multi-store pattern precedes it in the caller. Compliant.

After resuming from IPI_STOP (DDB/kdb exit), calls fence_i() unconditionally on the restarting hart because the kernel debugger might have set a breakpoint. This is the remote-hart complement to db_write_bytes() and kdb_cpu_sync_icache(). Compliant — correctly flushes any stale icache entries that may have resulted from another hart's debugger stores.

Implements the RISC-V spec sequence: local fence_i(), then fence() + sbi_remote_fence_i() to all other active harts. Pinned to current hart via sched_pin(). The va/sz parameters are unused (full fence.i, not range-restricted), which is conservative and safe. Compliant with the ISA-mandated cross-hart icache synchronization protocol.

Calls pmap_sync_icache() BEFORE storing the new executable PTE via pmap_store() at line 3468. This ordering (icache sync → PTE write) is architecturally correct: it ensures any stale icache entries from a previous mapping at this VA are flushed before the page becomes executable. The PTE store itself makes the new translation visible. Compliant.

The fence_i() inline emits 'fence.i' with a compiler memory clobber (::: "memory"). The memory clobber acts as a compiler barrier preventing reordering of stores across the fence_i() call. This is correct — it guarantees that all C-level stores before the fence_i() call are emitted as machine stores before the fence.i instruction in program order.
